title: Periodic Classification of Elements
summary: By the middle of the nineteenth century more than 60 elements were known, and studying each one separately was difficult. Like medicines arranged in a chemist's shop, elements were grouped so that similar ones could be studied together. The first classification, into metals and non-metals, failed because elements such as germanium and antimony show properties of both. After Prout's work (1815), atomic mass — a property that does not change — became the basis of classification.

J.W. Döbereiner grouped similar elements in threes (triads). When arranged by increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element is nearly the average of the other two, and its properties are in between: Li (7), Na (23), K (39); Ca (40), Sr (88), Ba (137); Cl (35.5), Br (80), I (127). Only a few triads could be found, so the idea was not widely accepted.

John Newlands arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found that every eighth element resembles the first, like the eighth note of a musical scale (Li and Na; Be, Mg and Ca; F and Cl). Merits: atomic mass was the basis and periodicity of properties was recognised for the first time. Demerits: it worked only up to calcium (atomic mass 40); after the noble gases were discovered the ninth element, not the eighth, resembled the first.

D. Mendeleev studied all 63 known elements and stated: the physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. His table has horizontal rows called periods (now 7) and vertical columns called groups (I to VIII, with A and B subgroups; group VIII has three elements in each of three periods; group zero was added for the noble gases). Elements in a group are chemically similar and show gradation from top to bottom; properties change regularly along a period. He gave more importance to properties than to atomic mass.

Merits: it included all known elements; atomic masses of some elements (Be, Au, In) were corrected; gaps were left for undiscovered elements whose properties he predicted — eka-silicon (germanium, discovered by Winkler in 1886), eka-boron (scandium) and eka-aluminium (gallium); group number gave the valency.

Defects: the position of hydrogen is uncertain (it resembles both alkali metals and halogens); isotopes have different masses but no separate places; anomalous pairs — a heavier element is placed before a lighter one (Co 58.9 before Ni 58.7, Te before I, Ar before K); dissimilar elements are grouped together (Cu and Ag with the alkali metals) and similar ones separated (Au and Pt).

In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that the atomic number, not the atomic mass, is the most fundamental property of an element. Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. Periodicity arises because similar electronic configurations recur: Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1), K (2,8,8,1) all have one valence electron, so all alkali metals are soft, very reactive, form M⁺ ions and basic oxides, and react with water to give hydrogen.
## The long form of the periodic table

It has 18 groups (1–18) and 7 periods (1–7). Elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties, while the number of shells increases down the group. Elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers; the period number equals the shell being filled (period 3: Na 2,8,1 to Ar 2,8,8). Period 1 has 2 elements (H, He); periods 2 and 3 are short (8 each); 4 and 5 are long (18 each); 6 and 7 are very long (32 each).

Main group (representative) elements: groups 1, 2 and 13–17. Noble gases (group 18): 8 valence electrons (He has 2), valency zero, almost inert, all gases. Transition elements (groups 3–12): metals with high melting and boiling points, good conductors, some magnetic, many used as catalysts, variable valency. Inner transition elements (lanthanoids 58–71 and actinoids 90–103) are shown separately below the table. Metals are on the left (alkali metals in group 1, alkaline earth metals in group 2); non-metals on the right (halogens in group 17, chalcogens in group 16); metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po) along a diagonal from boron to polonium.

Merits of the modern table: isotopes have the same atomic number and so the same place; anomalous pairs disappear (Co 27 comes before Ni 28); it is based on electronic configuration; metals, non-metals, metalloids and transition elements are clearly placed.

Atomic size (atomic radius, measured in picometres) is the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell. Across a period from left to right the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so they are pulled closer and atomic size decreases (Li is the largest and F the smallest in period 2). Down a group a new shell is added each time, so atomic size increases (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs).

Metallic (electropositive) character is the tendency to lose electrons and form cations; non-metallic (electronegative) character is the tendency to gain electrons. Metallic character decreases across a period (Na, Mg, Al metals; Si metalloid; P, S, Cl non-metals) and increases down a group (C non-metal; Si, Ge metalloids; Sn, Pb metals), because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and held less strongly. So potassium is more metallic than sodium.

vsa: Döbereiner arranged elements in triads. In one triad the atomic masses of lithium and potassium are 7 and 39. Identify the third element and explain how it supports the law of triads.

The third element is sodium (atomic mass 23). The average of 7 and 39 is (7 + 39)/2 = 23, which equals the atomic mass of sodium, the middle element; its properties are also in between those of lithium and potassium.
Mention any two limitations of Mendeleev's periodic table.

(1) Isotopes, which have different atomic masses, were not given separate places. (2) In some anomalous pairs a heavier element was placed before a lighter one, e.g. cobalt before nickel and argon before potassium. (Also: uncertain position of hydrogen; dissimilar elements grouped together.)
How do the following vary down a group: (a) the number of filled shells (b) the number of valence electrons (c) the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons?

(a) The number of filled shells increases by one in each step down the group. (b) The number of valence electrons stays the same. (c) The force of attraction decreases, because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.
How does (a) the force of attraction between the nucleus and valence electrons and (b) the atomic radius change in a period from left to right?

(a) The nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so the force of attraction on the valence electrons increases. (b) Because the electrons are pulled closer, the atomic radius decreases from left to right.

The physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers — when elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number, elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals.
Why do all elements of group 1 have similar chemical properties?

All group 1 elements (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1 …) have one electron in their outermost shell. Since chemical properties depend on the valence electrons, they all lose one electron easily, form M⁺ ions and show similar reactions.
sa: Elements A, B, C, D, E and F belong to the same period and have atomic radii 0.64 Å, 1.52 Å, 0.66 Å, 1.06 Å, 0.70 Å and 0.88 Å respectively (none is a noble gas). (a) Arrange them in increasing order of atomic number. (b) Name one metal and one non-metal among them. (c) Which is likely to form a strongly acidic oxide?

Atomic size decreases across a period as atomic number increases. (a) B (1.52) < D (1.06) < F (0.88) < E (0.70) < C (0.66) < A (0.64), i.e. B, D, F, E, C, A. (b) B (largest, on the left) is a metal; A (smallest, on the right) is a non-metal. (c) A, the most non-metallic, forms a strongly acidic oxide.
October 2024
How does the tendency to lose electrons change in the group of alkali metals, and why?

The tendency to lose electrons increases from lithium to caesium. Down the group a new shell is added each time, so the single valence electron is farther from the nucleus and is held less strongly (inner shells also shield it). It is therefore lost more easily, and metallic character and reactivity increase.
April 2026
What are metalloids and where are they placed in the modern periodic table? How does metallic character change (i) from top to bottom in a group and (ii) from left to right in a period?

Metalloids show properties of both metals and non-metals, e.g. boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic. They lie along a zig-zag diagonal from boron (group 13) down to polonium (group 16), between the metals on the left and the non-metals on the right. (i) Metallic character increases down a group because the valence electrons are lost more easily. (ii) It decreases from left to right across a period because the nucleus holds the valence electrons more strongly.
October 2021
What are transition elements? Where are they located in the modern periodic table? Write four characteristics of transition elements.

Transition elements are the elements of groups 3 to 12 in the middle block of the periodic table, whose two outermost shells are incomplete. Characteristics: (1) all are metals with high melting and boiling points; (2) good conductors of heat and electricity; (3) many act as catalysts; (4) they show variable valency (and some are attracted by a magnet).
April 2019
How does modern periodic law differ from Mendeleev's periodic law? Explain any two defects of Mendeleev's periodic table that were overcome in the modern table.

Mendeleev's law: properties are a periodic function of atomic mass. Modern law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number. Defects removed: (1) Isotopes — they have the same atomic number, so they now share one position. (2) Anomalous pairs — cobalt (27) naturally comes before nickel (28), and argon (18) before potassium (19), when arranged by atomic number.
October 2017
Describe any four main features of Mendeleev's periodic table.

(1) Elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic mass in horizontal rows (periods) and vertical columns (groups). (2) There are periods 1 to 6/7 and groups I to VIII (with a zero group added for noble gases); groups I–VII have A and B subgroups. (3) Elements in a group are chemically similar and show gradation in properties from top to bottom. (4) Gaps were left for undiscovered elements, whose properties were predicted (eka-silicon = germanium).

Define atomic size. How does atomic size change in a period and in a group? Where would the element with the largest atomic size be in (a) a group (b) a period?

Atomic size (radius) is the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an isolated atom. It decreases from left to right across a period (greater nuclear charge pulls electrons closer) and increases down a group (a new shell is added). (a) The largest atom is at the bottom of a group. (b) In a period it is at the extreme left (group 1).

la: State any three merits and three defects of Mendeleev's periodic table.

Merits: (1) all 63 known elements were classified, making their study systematic; (2) wrong atomic masses of some elements (Be, In, Au) were corrected from their positions; (3) gaps were left for undiscovered elements and their properties predicted — eka-silicon (germanium), eka-boron (scandium), eka-aluminium (gallium). Defects: (1) uncertain position of hydrogen, which resembles both alkali metals and halogens; (2) no separate places for isotopes; (3) anomalous pairs such as Co–Ni, Te–I and Ar–K, and grouping of dissimilar elements (Cu, Ag with Na, K) while separating similar ones (Au, Pt).

Part of the modern periodic table is given: group A — Li (3), Na (11), K (19), Rb (37); group B — Be (4), Mg (12), Ca (20), Sr (38). (a) Give the electronic configuration of Ca. (b) Write the number of valence electrons in K. (c) How many shells are there in Na? (d) Arrange the elements of group B in increasing order of atomic size. (e) Is Rb a metal or a non-metal? (f) Out of Na, Li, Be and Mg, which has the biggest atom?

(a) Ca: 2, 8, 8, 2. (b) K (2, 8, 8, 1) has 1 valence electron. (c) Na (2, 8, 1) has 3 shells. (d) Be < Mg < Ca < Sr (size increases down a group). (e) Rb is a metal (an alkali metal). (f) Na — it is lower in the group than Li and to the left of Mg in period 3.
Describe the long form of the modern periodic table in terms of groups and periods. What are main group elements, noble gases, transition elements and inner transition elements?

The table has 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods. Elements of a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties; down a group the number of shells increases. Elements of a period have consecutive atomic numbers and fill the same shell (period number = shell number); period 1 has 2 elements, periods 2–3 have 8, 4–5 have 18, 6–7 have 32. Main group elements: groups 1, 2 and 13–17, with incomplete outer shells. Noble gases: group 18, full outer shell, valency zero, inert gases. Transition elements: groups 3–12, metals with variable valency, used as catalysts. Inner transition elements: lanthanoids (58–71) and actinoids (90–103), shown separately below the table.

or: What is the common name of the group 18 elements of the modern periodic table? State their four characteristics.

They are called noble (inert) gases — He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn. (1) Their outermost shell has 8 electrons (helium has 2), a stable configuration. (2) Their valency is zero. (3) They hardly react and are almost inert. (4) All are gases at room temperature, present in small amounts in air.
